title: Cloudflare Pages & Workers
subtitle: Deploy to the world's largest edge network — unlimited bandwidth, Workers for backend logic, and R2 for storage

content.text: Cloudflare Pages is newer than Vercel and Netlify but has a compelling advantage: it runs on Cloudflare's network — 300+ cities worldwide, the same CDN that handles 20% of internet traffic. Free tier has unlimited bandwidth (Vercel and Netlify cap free tier). Cloudflare Workers (serverless functions at the edge) run in V8 isolates, not Node.js — cold starts are ~0ms. If you already use Cloudflare for DNS, adding Pages is seamless.

content.code:
# Install Wrangler (Cloudflare's CLI)
npm install -g wrangler

# Login
wrangler login

# Deploy a Pages project directly
wrangler pages deploy ./dist \
  --project-name my-react-app

# Or via GitHub integration:
# Cloudflare Dashboard → Pages → Create project → Connect to Git
# Same auto-build workflow as Vercel/Netlify

# Framework build settings (auto-detected or manual):
# React/Vite:   Build command: npm run build, Output: dist
# Next.js:      Build command: npm run build, Output: .vercel/output (with @cloudflare/next-on-pages)
# Astro:        Build command: npm run build, Output: dist

# Check deployment status
wrangler pages deployment list --project-name my-react-app

name = "my-worker"
main = "src/index.ts"
compatibility_date = "2024-01-01"

# KV Namespace binding
[[kv_namespaces]]
binding = "KV"
id = "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"

# R2 Bucket (like S3, but free egress)
[[r2_buckets]]
binding = "BUCKET"
bucket_name = "my-app-storage"

# D1 Database (SQLite at the edge — free tier)
[[d1_databases]]
binding = "DB"
database_name = "myapp-db"
database_id = "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"

# Secrets (set with 'wrangler secret put API_KEY')
# They appear as env.API_KEY in the worker

[vars]
NODE_ENV = "production"

content.text: R2 is S3 with zero egress cost. AWS charges $0.09/GB to download data from S3. Cloudflare R2 charges nothing for data downloads. For media-heavy apps (images, video, downloads), R2 can save significant money. R2 is S3-compatible — you can use the AWS SDK pointing at R2's endpoint, or use the native R2 bindings in Workers.

questions.question: A Cloudflare Worker runs at the edge. What does this mean for latency vs a traditional server in us-east-1?
options: No difference — network latency is the same regardless of where code runs
Workers run in 300+ cities — a Mumbai user's request is processed in Mumbai (< 10ms) instead of traveling to us-east-1 (150ms+)
Workers are slower because they share infrastructure
Workers are only deployed to US regions by default
questions.explanation: Edge computing means your code runs in the Cloudflare datacenter closest to the user. A Mumbai user's request is processed in Cloudflare's Mumbai PoP, not routed across the ocean to your VPS. This makes a massive difference for latency-sensitive operations: 5-20ms edge vs 150-300ms cross-continent. Cloudflare Workers are deployed globally by default — you write code once, it runs everywhere simultaneously.

faq.q: What are the limitations of Cloudflare Workers vs Node.js?
faq.a: Workers run in V8 isolates, not Node.js. This means: no Node.js built-in modules (no 'fs', 'path', 'crypto' — use Web Crypto API instead), limited npm package compatibility (packages using Node.js internals don't work), 128MB memory limit, and 50ms CPU time on the free plan (paid: 30s). Workers use Web APIs (fetch, Request, Response, URL) — the same APIs as modern browser JavaScript. Most npm packages designed for the web (not Node.js) work fine.

examples: Shopify uses Cloudflare Workers to run storefront logic at the edge for their millions of merchants. When a customer visits a Shopify store, the initial HTML is rendered by a Worker in their city — dramatically reducing time-to-first-byte
Linear (project management tool) serves their entire frontend from Cloudflare Pages with Workers for API middleware. Their time-to-interactive is < 500ms globally because everything is edge-first
